parts.label: (a)
hints: Hint 1: Think about what happens to an analogue signal as it travels - any extra unwanted voltage just adds on and cannot be separated. What is special about a digital signal that only has two levels, high and low?

Hint 2: Think of two extra things you can do with numbers that you cannot do with a smooth varying voltage - for example checking for mistakes, scrambling for security, or squeezing more information together.
parts.proper_answer: Any two from: noise can be removed and signal regenerated; extra bits can be added for error checking/correction; signal can be encrypted for increased security; data compression and multiplexing are possible.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Why digital is tougher against noise**
Think of an analogue signal as a smooth hill where every tiny height matters. If noise adds a little extra voltage, the shape is permanently changed. A digital signal only cares whether the voltage is high (1) or low (0), so even if noise wobbles it a little, the receiver can still tell 1 from 0 and rebuild a perfect clean copy. This is called regeneration.

Step 2: **What else numbers let you do**
Once your sound is just numbers, you can do clever maths on it. You can add extra parity bits to detect and correct errors, encrypt the numbers so only the intended receiver can decode them, compress the data to use less bandwidth, and interleave (multiplex) many signals on the same line. Pick any two of these ideas for your two marks.

parts.label: (b)(i)
hints: Hint 1: First work out how often samples are taken from $f = 250\text{ Hz}$, then read the p.d. values off Fig. 5.2 at 4 ms and 8 ms and remember 1 mV = 1 in binary.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Find the sampling interval**
Sampling frequency tells you samples per second. The time between samples is: $$T = \frac{1}{f} = \frac{1}{250} = 0.004\text{ s} = 4\text{ ms}$$ So samples are at 0, 4 ms, 8 ms, 12 ms, and so on. You are already told time 0 is 0001, which is 1, matching $\approx 1\text{ mV}$ on Fig. 5.2.

Step 2: **Read the graph and convert to 4-bit binary**
At 4 ms Fig. 5.2 reads $5\text{ mV}$. With LSB = $1\text{ mV}$, the number is 5. In 4-bit binary: $$5 = 4+1 = 0101$$ At 8 ms Fig. 5.2 reads $4\text{ mV}$. The number is 4: $$4 = 0100$$ So 4 ms: 0101, 8 ms: 0100.

parts.label: (b)(ii)
hints: Hint 1: Remember what a DAC does - it holds each sampled voltage constant until the next sample arrives. Look at Fig. 5.3 and see how long the 5 mV level from the 4 ms sample should last.
Hint 2: Check what value the next sample at 8 ms has from part (b)(i), and think what horizontal level the trace must drop or rise to after 8 ms.
parts.proper_answer: The 5 mV level continues horizontally from 6 ms to 8 ms, then drops vertically at 8 ms to 4 mV and continues horizontally at 4 mV to 12 ms.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Understand sample-and-hold**
The DAC does not recreate the smooth curve. It outputs the last received number as a steady d.c. level until a new number arrives. Since samples are 4 ms apart, each horizontal step is 4 ms wide.

Step 2: **Complete the staircase**
Fig. 5.3 already shows 1 mV from 0 to 4 ms and 5 mV from 4 to 6 ms. The 5 mV sample taken at 4 ms must be held for the full interval: $$4\text{ ms to }8\text{ ms at }5\text{ mV}$$ At 8 ms the new sample is 4 mV, so draw a vertical drop at 8 ms then: $$8\text{ ms to }12\text{ ms at }4\text{ mV}$$ This gives the characteristic blocky reconstructed signal.

parts.label: (c)
hints: Hint 1: Start by converting the new sampling frequency to a new time between samples, to find how wide each flat step will now be.
Hint 2: Now think about the new voltage step size - with LSB = 2 mV the DAC can only output even numbers 0, 2, 4, 6 mV, so each smooth reading must be rounded down to the nearest even value.
Hint 3: Read Fig. 5.2 at each new sampling time 0, 2, 4, 6, 8, 10 ms and decide which allowed level 0, 2, 4 or 6 mV each one will be held at.
parts.proper_answer: Steps of width 2 ms. Levels held from each sample time: 0 to 2 ms at 0 mV, 2 to 4 ms at 2 mV, 4 to 6 ms at 4 mV, 6 to 8 ms at 6 mV, 8 to 10 ms at 4 mV, 10 to 12 ms at 6 mV.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **New sampling interval**
$$T = \frac{1}{f} = \frac{1}{500} = 0.002\text{ s} = 2\text{ ms}$$ So you now sample twice as often, at 0, 2, 4, 6, 8, 10, 12 ms. Each DAC output step will be only 2 ms wide, giving better time detail.

Step 2: **New voltage resolution**
3-bit with LSB = $2\text{ mV}$ means allowed outputs are multiples of 2 mV: 0, 2, 4, 6 mV, etc. This is coarser in voltage. The ADC rounds down to the nearest allowed level.

Step 3: **Read and quantise each sample**
From Fig. 5.2 approximately: 0 ms $\approx 1\text{ mV}$ goes to 0 mV, 2 ms $\approx 2\text{ mV}$ goes to 2 mV, 4 ms $\approx 5\text{ mV}$ goes to 4 mV, 6 ms $\approx 7\text{ mV}$ goes to 6 mV, 8 ms $= 4\text{ mV}$ stays at 4 mV, 10 ms $= 6\text{ mV}$ stays at 6 mV. Draw horizontal steps of width 2 ms at those heights. More steps but chunkier heights - higher sampling rate but lower voltage resolution.
